output.direct_findings: [S1] In a controlled 3D study of 20 light-weight male freestyle wrestlers, elite wrestlers reached the opponent’s legs with a shorter time-to-peak trailing-limb ground-reaction force and greater peak resultant force, while showing greater early forward velocity/displacement of the upper body; peak whole-body forward velocity and movement duration did not differ significantly. The authors characterize the double-leg attack as a sequence of approach/lowering, forward upper-body drive, leg capture, and completion of the takedown. [S1] [S2] Wrestling is an intermittent grappling sport involving sudden attacks, counterattacks, and control phases; the review evidence identifies anaerobic power/capacity, aerobic fitness for sustaining effort and recovery, maximal dynamic and isometric strength, explosive strength, and strength endurance as performance-relevant attributes. [S2] [S3] The physiological systematic review reports large pre/post-bout changes in heart rate, blood lactate, and selected bear-hug and handgrip measures, supporting substantial acute cardiovascular, metabolic, and neuromuscular demand during competitive bouts. [S3] [S4] Sport-specific test evidence in Olympic combat sports is heterogeneous: many studies have small samples and incomplete familiarization, reliability, validity, sensitivity, or feasibility reporting; therefore, test outputs should not be treated as universally validated proxies for match success. [S4] [S5] A repeated Wrestling-Specific Fitness Test using 3-minute throwing rounds produced differentiation between youth quality categories in selected performance variables, but this is evidence for that test and population, not proof that its scores generalize to all wrestling styles, ages, weights, or competition contexts.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent Wrestling as high-intensity intermittent grappling with distinct control/engagement, attack or counterattack, takedown/throw, and recovery/inter-period phases rather than as continuous steady-state locomotion. High-confidence correction: include both anaerobic burst actions and aerobic contribution to sustained effort and recovery; do not encode a single exclusive energy-system label. High-confidence correction: movement records for a double-leg attack may include approach/lowering, rapid upper-body projection, trailing-foot propulsion, leg capture, and takedown completion, with force timing and early upper-body velocity as biomechanical features when the event is specifically a freestyle leg attack [S1]. Inference—planning only: these phases can motivate separate model states or event labels, but the cited study does not establish universal phase durations, action frequencies, or transfer to every wrestling style. Inference—planning only: conditioning relevance can be represented as broad qualities (explosive/ maximal/isometric strength, strength endurance, anaerobic capacity, aerobic recovery), but the evidence does not justify individualized prescriptions, exact load ratios, or claims that a single test predicts competitive performance. Boundary: S1 is a small, light-weight male freestyle sample and should not be generalized without qualification to Greco-Roman, women’s, youth, or heavier-weight profiles; S5 is youth-specific and test-specific.

output.direct_findings: [S1] NCAA Division I game demands differ significantly by position: wide receivers and defensive backs recorded greater total distance, high-intensity running, sprint distance, and high-intensity acceleration/deceleration efforts than their respective position groups. [S2] In a three-year NFL sample, wide receivers, cornerbacks, and safeties recorded the greatest game distances and maximum velocities, whereas offensive linemen recorded the lowest; linemen also showed fewer high-velocity efforts. [S2] The NFL tracking study quantified acceleration and deceleration as distinct locomotor events and found the greatest high-threshold deceleration distances in wide receivers and defensive backs, with substantially lower values in linemen. [S2] Across the literature summarized by the NFL study, linemen accumulate less running distance and high-velocity distance but more collision/contact activity than non-linemen. [S3] In the eligible American-football study, high-intensity accelerations occurred more frequently than high-intensity decelerations; the review also found a small reduction in high- and very-high-intensity acceleration and deceleration frequencies from the first to second half, but American football was represented by only one study. [S4] American football combines high-velocity movement with frequent collisions, and external workload differs materially between positions and between training and competition. [S5] American football is characterized as intermittent and position-specific rather than a continuous, uniform running sport, with physical requirements spanning short intense actions, recovery periods, and contact-related demands.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent American football as an intermittent, position-conditioned sport rather than using one homogeneous movement profile. High-confidence correction: retain separate channels for total distance, velocity exposure, acceleration, deceleration, and contact/collision exposure; running metrics alone do not represent linemen's demands. High-confidence correction: encode major action phases as play onset/short explosive locomotion, rapid acceleration or braking/change of direction, position-specific skill/contact engagement, and between-play recovery, while allowing role-specific phase weights. Inference for planning: use position- and competition-level stratification before calibrating workload or conditioning relevance; the cited studies support this stratification but do not establish that any particular training prescription transfers to performance or reduces injury risk. Boundary: do not infer individual workload targets, injury probability, or medical/training decisions from these group-level observational data; GPS/LPS thresholds and on-field versus player-game inclusion can materially change estimates.
output.sources: [S1] Quantification of Competitive Game Demands of NCAA Division I College Football Players | https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26382134/ | primary observational GPS/accelerometry study; [S2] Positional Movement Demands during NFL Football Games: A 3-Year Review | https://doi.org/10.3390/app13169278 | primary observational player-tracking study; [S3] High-Intensity Acceleration and Deceleration Demands in Elite Team Sports Competitive Match Play: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies | https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-019-01170-1 | systematic review and meta-analysis; [S4] A Narrative Review of the Physical Demands and Injury Incidence in American Football: Application of Current Knowledge and Practices in Workload Management | https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0783-2 | sport-specific narrative review; [S5] A Physiological Review of American Football | https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-199723040-00004 | foundational sport-physiology review

output.direct_findings: [S1] Across 35 studies, basketball demands vary by competition level; elite players generally covered less distance at lower average velocities than sub-elite and youth players, while retaining a greater capacity to express high-velocity movement. The review also identifies acceleration, deceleration, change of direction, jumping, and shuffling as central basketball actions, but concludes that acceleration/deceleration evidence remains insufficiently standardized. [S2] Across 25 match-play studies, players covered approximately 5–6 km during live play in 40-minute matches, with average physiological intensity above lactate threshold and above 85% of maximal heart rate; vigorous activity decreased late in matches. Guards sprinted and performed high-intensity shuffling more often than forwards and centers, with positional and level-related variation. [S3] In 20 trained junior second-league players, jump shots and countermovement jumps produced high lower-limb mean and peak power; the jump-shot task included measurable take-off and landing forces, and the authors reported high landing forces alongside evidence of soft-landing behavior in this sample. [S4] In one NCAA Division I men's team observed over two seasons, IMU-derived game loads were associated with selected game statistics, and training loads two days before games were associated with subsequent game loads; the authors note that commonly used inertial metrics differ in validation status, with PlayerLoad better established than some Inertial Movement Analysis measures.
output.model_implications: Use a basketball movement model that represents intermittent, multidirectional sequences rather than continuous straight-line running: acceleration, deceleration, cutting/change of direction, shuffling, jumping, landing, and brief high-intensity bouts. [Direct evidence: S1–S3] Preserve contextual fields for playing position, competition level, sex, match period, and live-play exposure because these materially modify observed demands. [Direct evidence: S1–S2] Treat exact acceleration/deceleration counts, universal work-to-rest ratios, and fixed positional load targets as uncertain unless the source dataset specifies tracking technology, thresholds, competition format, and playing time. [Direct evidence: S1–S2] Treat IMU PlayerLoad/IMA as device- and algorithm-dependent measurement variables, not interchangeable physiological or biomechanical ground truth. [Direct evidence: S4] Inference: conditioning-relevance tags may prioritize repeated high-intensity multidirectional actions and explosive jump/landing phases, but the evidence does not justify claiming that a modeled drill or metric transfers directly to basketball performance. Inference: any movement-record schema should separate observed external load, internal response, technical action, and contextual exposure rather than collapsing them into one generic intensity score.
output.sources: Training load and match-play demands in basketball based on competition level: a systematic review | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0229212 | systematic review; The activity demands and physiological responses encountered during basketball match-play: a systematic review | https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0794-z | systematic review; Biomechanical Analysis of the Jump Shot in Basketball | https://doi.org/10.2478/hukin-2014-0062 | primary laboratory biomechanics study; Biomechanical Loads and Their Effects on Player Performance in Basketball | https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2021.670018 | primary observational longitudinal study using IMU/tracking and game statistics

output.direct_findings: [S1] Across 30 studies, no consensus exists for absolute high-speed-running or sprint thresholds in professional adult soccer. Reported official-match ranges were 618–1,001 m of high-speed running and 153–295 m of sprinting in professional men, and 911–1,063 m and 223–307 m, respectively, in professional women. [S1] Soccer match play is intermittent, combining accelerations, decelerations, changes of direction, sprinting, jumping, and tackling with standing, walking, and jogging recovery. [S2] Horizontal decelerations have high-impact peak ground-reaction forces and loading rates, with the greatest forces occurring early in stance (<50 ms); peak forces can be up to 2.7 times those in the first steps of maximal horizontal acceleration. [S3] In 10 competitive matches involving 23 elite players, transitional-play demands differed by position: central attacking midfielders had higher total-distance rates, fullbacks the highest sprint-distance rates, wingers the highest high-intensity acceleration/deceleration frequency, and centre backs generally the lowest outputs; attackers showed the highest metrics during high-pressure activities. [S4] In video analysis of 360 goals from Germany’s first national league, 83% were preceded by at least one powerful action by the scorer or assister; straight sprinting was the most frequent action for both scorers and assisters, although the study describes association with goal situations, not causal performance benefit.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent soccer movement as intermittent and multidirectional, with separate event types for acceleration, deceleration, change of direction, sprint, jump, tackle, and low-intensity recovery rather than a single continuous-running variable. High-confidence correction: store speed-threshold definitions and tracking method as metadata; do not hard-code one universal high-speed or sprint threshold because the review found substantial heterogeneity and no consensus. High-confidence correction: include positional role and match phase/transition context as conditioning variables for movement-demand records. Inference: deceleration should carry a distinct mechanical-load label from acceleration, but the cited review does not establish a universal per-event load coefficient for soccer. Inference: straight sprinting is a relevant action-phase feature for goal-context records, but it should not be encoded as a universal determinant of scoring or as proof that training transfer occurs. Boundary: these sources support descriptive calibration of elite 11-a-side soccer movement records; they do not justify individualized medical, injury-risk, or training prescriptions, nor direct transfer claims from drills to match performance.
output.sources: High-speed running and sprinting in professional adult soccer: Current thresholds definition, match demands and training strategies | https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2023.1116293 | systematic review; Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Acceleration and Deceleration in Multidirectional Sports | https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01693-0 | systematic review; Physical match demands across different playing positions during transitional play and high-pressure activities in elite soccer | https://doi.org/10.5114/biolsport.2024.131815 | primary observational study; Straight sprinting is the most frequent action in goal situations in professional football | https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2012.665940 | primary video-analysis study

output.direct_findings: [S1] The baseball swing is a sequential, rotational action: rear-foot weight shift and trunk coil are followed by a forward stride, front-foot force application, hip rotation, shoulder rotation, and bat acceleration. In this study, front-foot force reached 123% of body weight, peak hip rotation was 714°/s, peak shoulder-segment velocity was 937°/s, and peak linear bat velocity was 31 m/s. [S2] Pitching evidence links performance and upper-extremity kinetics to coordinated lower-body contribution, lead-leg braking, pelvis and trunk rotation timing, shoulder positioning, and arm acceleration; the review describes meaningful differences by pitch type and reports that fatigue was accompanied by increased arm pain despite largely stable kinetic values. [S3] Pitching is commonly organized into wind-up, stride, arm-cocking, acceleration, deceleration, and follow-through phases; laboratory kinematic variables have been linked to joint loading, but the review does not establish that one universally optimal technique or a generic conditioning program prevents injury. [S4] The systematic review/meta-analysis provides normative adult-pitching mechanics data and supports treating pitching kinematics as reference distributions rather than single target values. [S5] MLB position-player workloads differ by defensive position: outfielders showed the highest high-speed running, infielders and catchers lower running demands, middle infielders the highest total throws, and shortstops/third basemen the highest hard-throw volumes; offensive and baserunning metrics were broadly similar across positions in the analyzed cohort.
output.model_implications: Represent Baseball as a role- and event-dependent profile rather than a single movement signature: pitcher, catcher, infielder, and outfielder records should have distinct workload channels. This is a high-confidence calibration correction because position-specific running and throwing differences were directly observed in MLB Statcast data [S5]. Encode pitching as a phase sequence—wind-up, stride, arm-cocking, acceleration, deceleration, follow-through—and hitting as a rotational kinetic-chain sequence with explicit stride/foot-contact, pelvis/trunk rotation, and bat-acceleration events [S1] [S3]. This is a high-confidence representation correction, not a claim that every athlete uses identical phase timing. Store pitching and hitting kinematic variables as distributions with population, level, position, and pitch/swing context, rather than universal thresholds; this is an inference grounded in the systematic-review emphasis on normative ranges and methodological variation [S2] [S4]. Treat conditioning relevance as task-demand mapping—short high-speed running and acceleration, repeated throwing, explosive rotation, and position-specific volume—rather than direct proof that a particular exercise transfers to performance or reduces injury; this boundary is an inference from the demand studies and reviews [S1] [S2] [S5]. Do not encode causal claims that a listed kinematic feature alone predicts injury, that fatigue always increases joint kinetics, or that a generic conditioning intervention prevents injury; the cited evidence is correlational/review-based and context-dependent.
output.sources: [S1] Hitting a baseball: a biomechanical description | https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8580946/ | primary 3-D kinematic/kinetic study; [S2] Baseball Pitching Biomechanics in Relation to Injury Risk and Performance | https://doi.org/10.1177/1941738109338546 | systematic narrative review of original studies; [S3] Baseball pitching kinematics, joint loads, and injury prevention: a review | https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2095254612000427 | biomechanics/injury-prevention review; [S4] Pitching mechanics and performance of adult baseball pitchers: A systematic review and meta-analysis for normative data | https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2022.11.004 | systematic review and meta-analysis; [S5] In-game workload demands of position players in Major League Baseball | https://doi.org/10.1177/19417381231179970 | observational cohort study using MLB Statcast data

output.direct_findings: [S1] For sprint events up to 400 m, the start comprises the block phase followed by early flight and stance phases; higher-performing starts are associated with greater block force production, shorter first-flight duration, longer first-stance contact, and important ankle/knee energy-generation features. [S2] Across 109 track-and-field sprint studies, sprint-start performance is associated with center-of-mass position, block force, and rapid force production; acceleration involves step-length/frequency transition, propulsive force, and reduced braking force; constant-speed running emphasizes force orientation and deceleration involves lower step frequency and longer contact time. [S3] In a small sample of 13 participants, mean 100-m speed correlated with mechanical power, a velocity-oriented force–velocity profile, backward-directed resultant-force application during acceleration, and higher step frequency/shorter contact time; resultant-force magnitude alone, aerial time, and step length were not significant correlates in that study. [S4] World Athletics’ official biomechanical studies provide competition-based measurements across selected track and field events, including split times, kinematics, and event-specific performance parameters; they are observational competition resources rather than controlled conditioning trials. [S5] Running style can be represented parsimoniously using step frequency and duty factor at a given speed, with ground-reaction-force and whole-body-kinematic interpretation tied to those spatiotemporal variables.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent Track and field as a multi-event profile rather than one homogeneous movement pattern; at minimum separate sprint/hurdles, middle/long-distance running, jumps, throws, and combined events. High-confidence correction: for sprint records, encode event phase explicitly—block/start, acceleration, maximal or constant-speed running, and deceleration/finish—and retain contact time, flight time, step frequency, force direction, and power as distinct variables rather than treating “speed” as a single biomechanical construct. High-confidence boundary: do not infer that a single optimal set position, step length, peak force, or technique applies to every athlete or every athletics event; the reviews report heterogeneity and unresolved roles for body configuration, strength, sex, age, and measurement methods [S1] [S2]. Planning inference: conditioning relevance may be mapped to rapid force production, force orientation, elastic/stiff stance behavior, and event-specific repetition/duration demands, but these sources do not establish individualized training prescriptions or causal transfer from a generic exercise to competition performance. Planning inference: jump and throw movement records should use event-specific phases such as approach/penultimate-takeoff-flight-landing or preliminary movement/transition-delivery-release, but the cited sprint evidence must not be used as direct validation for those phase labels; use the governing-body reports or dedicated event studies for calibration. Data-model boundary: preserve measurement context—surface, device, speed, distance, competition versus laboratory/treadmill setting, athlete level, sex, and event—because associations from the 13-person sprint study and heterogeneous systematic-review literature should not be treated as universal causal parameters [S2] [S3].
output.sources: [S1] The Biomechanics of the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Narrative Review | https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-019-01138-1 | peer-reviewed narrative review; [S2] Determinant biomechanical variables for each sprint phase performance in track and field: A systematic review | https://doi.org/10.1177/17479541231200526 | peer-reviewed systematic review of 109 studies; [S3] Mechanical determinants of 100-m sprint running performance | https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-012-2379-8 | primary laboratory/field-correlational biomechanics study; [S4] Research Centre: Official Documents—World Athletics Biomechanical Studies | https://worldathletics.org/about-iaaf/documents/research-centre | governing-body competition biomechanics resource; [S5] The biomechanics of running and running styles: a synthesis | https://doi.org/10.1080/14763141.2021.1873411 | peer-reviewed synthetic review

output.direct_findings: [Kwok et al., 2021] Competitive swimming performance is usefully partitioned into start, stroking, and turn phases; in front crawl, strength/resistance and core-training interventions generally improved sprint performance and/or stroke-biomechanics measures, resistance training supported stroke rate, and plyometric training supported start performance, while evidence for turn improvement and transfer to overall performance was insufficient or inconsistent. [Vantorre et al., 2014] The swim start comprises preparation and block impulse, flight/water entry, underwater glide and kicking, and transition to breakout/full swimming; relevant measured variables include reaction/block time, take-off impulse, flight and underwater time, streamlined posture, resistance, and transition timing. Start expertise is distinct from general stroke expertise. [Gonjo and Olstad, 2020] In a primary study of 14 national-level male butterfly swimmers, mean underwater velocity was strongly related to start and turn segment times (r=-0.70 and -0.95); start and turn underwater segments used different kinematic strategies, and underwater distance/time alone did not explain performance. [Costa et al., 2015] A review of 34 longitudinal studies in adult elite swimmers found mixed physiological adaptation results across blood, endocrine, muscle-biochemistry, cardiovascular, and energetic outcomes; macro-level changes were limited and dependent on training background and experience, while study heterogeneity constrained generalization.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent swimming race movement records as at least start, clean-swimming/stroke-cycle, turn, and finish segments rather than as one undifferentiated locomotor action [Kwok et al., 2021] [Gonjo and Olstad, 2020]. High-confidence correction: for starts and turns, store phase-specific underwater variables—initial velocity, underwater velocity, breakout distance/time, kick timing or frequency, and transition/breakout timing—while preserving stroke/event labels; do not treat underwater distance or time as sufficient standalone performance descriptors [Vantorre et al., 2014] [Gonjo and Olstad, 2020]. High-confidence boundary: separate front-crawl or butterfly evidence from breaststroke/backstroke and from generic 'swimming'; the cited intervention synthesis is primarily front crawl, and the primary segment study is butterfly. Planning inference—not direct fact: dry-land strength, resistance, core, or plyometric records should be linked to swimming outcomes only through explicitly labeled, event- and phase-specific associations; do not encode universal transfer to race performance. Planning inference—not direct fact: conditioning relevance should be modeled as a contextual modifier (event distance, stroke, athlete level, training background), not as a fixed causal mapping from a land exercise to a swimming movement.

output.direct_findings: [S1] Tennis serve and groundstroke biomechanics vary with stroke type, direction, and stance style; the review identified 23 eligible biomechanical studies but reported inconsistent results associated with differences in player age, sex, performance level, measurement systems, and outcome definitions. [S1] The principal stroke categories represented include flat, slice, and topspin serves; longline and cross-court directions; and open, square, neutral, foot-up, and foot-back stance variants. [S2] In international singles match-play samples, pooled mean rally duration was approximately 5.5 s for men and 6.4 s for women, running distance per point approximately 9.6 m and 8.2 m, and effective playing time approximately 18.6% and 20%, respectively; estimates varied by sex, surface, and playing level. [S3] The tennis serve can be represented by three functional phases—preparation, acceleration, and follow-through—and eight stages; the phases correspond to energy storage, energy release, and deceleration. [S3] The serve is a whole-body sequential action involving segmental rotations and transfer through the kinetic chain, so isolated-joint descriptions do not fully represent the movement. [S4] Match play is intermittent, combining brief high- or near-maximal work bouts with longer low-to-moderate recovery periods; reported activity is affected by player level, style, sex, court surface, scoring/match format, and ball characteristics. [S4] The review reports typical work bouts of roughly 4–10 s, short recovery bouts of roughly 10–20 s, and longer interruptions of roughly 60–90 s under standard match conditions.
output.model_implications: Use separate movement/action labels for serve, forehand, backhand, volley/overhead, recovery, and directional-transition events rather than treating tennis as continuous running. [Inference] Represent the serve as preparation → acceleration/contact → follow-through/deceleration, while retaining optional sub-stages only when the source or sensor annotation supports them. [Inference] Model tennis as intermittent, multidirectional activity with context fields for surface, singles/doubles, sex category, competition level, rally/point format, and stroke/stance type; do not use one universal distance, rally duration, or work-rest constant. [Inference] Treat “conditioning relevance” as a planning hypothesis derived from the observed intermittent and multidirectional demands, not as direct proof that a particular exercise or program transfers to match performance. Do not encode causal injury-risk claims, individualized prescriptions, or exact joint-load thresholds from these sources. High-confidence correction: avoid collapsing all serve and groundstroke variants into a single biomechanical template. High-confidence correction: preserve measurement provenance and units because the review identifies substantial heterogeneity across force plates, pressure insoles, motion capture, video, and IMU methods. High-confidence boundary: wheelchair tennis, junior tennis, injured populations, and non-singles formats should not inherit these estimates without separate evidence.
output.sources: [S1] Biomechanical analyses of different serve and groundstroke techniques in tennis: A systematic scoping review | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0290320 | systematic scoping review; [S2] Physical Demands of Tennis Across the Different Court Surfaces, Performance Levels and Sexes: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis | https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01807-8 | systematic review and meta-analysis; [S3] An 8-Stage Model for Evaluating the Tennis Serve: Implications for Performance Enhancement and Injury Prevention | https://doi.org/10.1177/1941738111414175 | biomechanical evidence synthesis/descriptive model; [S4] Intensity of tennis match play | https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsm.2005.023168 | sport-performance and physiological review

output.direct_findings: [S1] Across 28 indoor-volleyball match-load studies, setters performed the greatest jump volumes, while middle blockers and outside/opposite hitters performed the most high jumps (>50 cm); internal load varied by position, and the review reported sex-related differences in jump count, height, and perceived exertion. [S2] In the included multi-directional-sport literature, volleyball was reported to require substantial jumping, with up to approximately 35 jumps per match in the reviewed studies; demand estimates varied by sex, age, and competition level, and practice loads were not represented. [S3] In 14 collegiate women, spike trials produced greater shoulder and elbow forces, torques, and angular velocities than roll shots and float serves; shoulder abduction at ball contact was approximately 130° across tested skills. [S4] In 30 male participants, experienced volleyball players used greater ankle dorsiflexion range during landings than novices; experienced players also showed greater plantarflexion at initial contact in spike jumps and greater knee-flexion range in block jumps, while peak vertical ground reaction force and loading rate did not differ. [S5] A survey of 30 coaches and 30 players found that strength and conditioning was viewed as important to volleyball skills, fitness, and injury-related parameters, but also documented a theory-to-practice gap and practical constraints; this is evidence of reported practice and perceptions, not proof that a particular program improves performance or prevents injury.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent indoor volleyball as an intermittent, court-based sport with repeated explosive jumps, overhead spike/serve actions, blocks, short multidirectional movements, and landing events rather than as a continuous running sport. High-confidence correction: preserve playing-position as a conditioning/load dimension because jump volume, high-jump exposure, and internal load differ by role [S1]. High-confidence correction: model jump count and jump height as separate variables; the evidence does not justify collapsing them into a single generic jump-load value [S1] [S2]. High-confidence correction: include action-phase labels for approach/take-off, aerial spike or block, and landing, while keeping overhead shoulder/elbow kinetics distinct from lower-limb landing kinetics [S3] [S4]. Inference for planning only: strength, power, speed, plyometric, and landing-focused conditioning are relevant categories because they map onto observed volleyball actions, but these sources do not establish a universal dose, causal transfer to match performance, or individualized injury-prevention prescription. Boundary: do not generalize indoor match-load values to beach volleyball, training sessions, youth athletes, or every sex/level/position without separate evidence.

output.direct_findings: Elite boxers produced higher lead-straight punch velocity, force, impulse, and rate-of-force-development indices than junior boxers; lead-leg start-up force indices were also higher, while rear-leg force-index differences were not significant [B1]. Across maximal bag punches, punch type materially changed the measured mechanics: the lead hook had the highest peak fist velocity, the jab the shortest delivery time, and uppercuts showed the highest reported shoulder or elbow angular-velocity values depending on hand/technique [B2]. In a separate elite-versus-junior sample, elite boxers produced greater force and velocity for the cross, hook, and uppercut, while juniors showed greater relative shoulder contribution; the cross displayed front/rear ground-reaction-force imbalance in both groups [B3]. The acute amateur-boxing literature shows large increases in blood lactate and several biochemical or endocrine markers after boxing-specific activity; responses were generally greater in competition than sparring and greater in sparring than simulation, while neuromuscular or task-specific performance did not consistently decline [B4]. Reviews characterize boxing as involving brief, dynamic punches and report broad relevance of cardiorespiratory fitness, anaerobic power, and upper- and lower-limb strength/power, but note heterogeneity and limited evidence for some attributes [B5].
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent boxing punches as technique-specific actions rather than one generic punch class; at minimum distinguish jab/straight, hook, and uppercut, and retain lead/rear-hand labels [B2] [B3]. High-confidence correction: encode a proximal-to-distal, whole-body kinetic-chain structure and permit force/velocity/RFD and lead/rear-leg contribution features when the measurement system supports them [B1] [B3]. High-confidence correction: separate isolated maximal-bag biomechanics from live-bout movement records and do not use laboratory punch velocity or force as direct proxies for competitive success [B1] [B2] [B3]. High-confidence correction: distinguish bout, sparring, and simulation contexts when modeling acute physiological load or recovery-state variables [B4]. output.direct_findings: [S1] The MMA literature spans injury, weight loss, technical/tactical analysis, fitness, physiological responses/training characteristics, psychobiology, and interventions; 112 eligible studies included 20,784 participants, but implementation studies testing real-world performance interventions were not identified. [S2] MMA combines striking and grappling; across the underpinning combat-sport literature, higher-level performance is associated with strength/neuromuscular power and anaerobic qualities, while superior aerobic power is not consistently present. Grappling success is more characterized by high-force and longer-duration anaerobic demands, whereas striking success is more associated with shorter-duration, higher-velocity actions. [S3] In a small male-comparator sample, higher-level MMA competitors performed better across most short-term anaerobic, repeated-maximal-effort, and intermittent-aerobic tests; lower short-term anaerobic performance or higher intermittent-endurance capacity was associated with a greater likelihood of bouts reaching a decision. [S4] In four simulated bouts of three 5-minute rounds separated by 1-minute rests, offensive actions and physiological/RPE responses varied by weight class and competitive level; lightweight athletes tended to show increasing physiological demand as the combat progressed. [S5] MMA time-motion research frames competition as alternating high-intensity combat actions and lower-activity periods across standing and ground exchanges, supporting analysis by action phase rather than treating a bout as continuous uniform effort.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent MMA as a hybrid striking–grappling sport with distinct but interacting action phases, at minimum separating striking exchanges, clinch/takedown/control transitions, ground grappling/submission work, and recovery/low-activity intervals; this is an evidence-aligned categorical model, not a claim that every bout follows the same sequence. High-confidence correction: permit intermittent high-intensity actions and repeated-effort demands alongside aerobic/intermittent-endurance variables; do not model MMA as purely aerobic or purely anaerobic. High-confidence correction: attach round structure and rule-set metadata because the directly studied simulation used three 5-minute rounds with 1-minute rests, while real competitions can vary by bout format. Inference for planning only: conditioning or movement records may map to acceleration, braking, forceful contact, high-velocity striking, repeated efforts, and positional control, but the cited evidence does not establish a universal movement-to-performance transfer function. Inference for planning only: weighting action phases by fighter style, opponent, weight class, competitive level, and bout outcome is reasonable, but no fixed phase proportions or universal intensity percentages should be hard-coded from this evidence. Boundary: direct MMA biomechanics evidence remains comparatively sparse; do not import punch/kick force values, joint-load thresholds, or injury-risk causal rules from boxing, kickboxing, wrestling, or laboratory drills without separate sport- and task-specific validation. Boundary: the strongest physiological findings are mostly male adult samples and small or heterogeneous cohorts, limiting generalization across sex, age, rules, and competition level.

output.direct_findings: [S1] Brazilian jiu-jitsu is intermittent, with high-, moderate-, and low-intensity actions interspersed; reported match duration varies by belt/category, and athletes may complete approximately four to six matches in a competition day. [S1] Across the reviewed literature, VO2max was approximately 42–52 mL/kg/min and aerobic fitness did not consistently discriminate competitive level; maximal dynamic, isometric, and endurance strength were associated with performance, while sport-specific power evidence was comparatively limited. [S1] Competition begins standing but most combat occurs in groundwork; recurrent scoring-relevant actions include takedowns, guard passes, mounts, back control, knee-on-belly, and sweeps, with submissions via chokes or joint locks as decisive outcomes. [S2] In regional-level competition, the study measured physiological responses alongside technical-tactical parameters, and its conclusions were explicitly limited to that competition level and sample. [S3] In four simulated 10-minute matches, successive bouts reduced maximal isometric handgrip strength after matches 3 and 4, while effort-pause structure and reported effort/recovery did not significantly change; the sample was only 10 athletes. [S4] The reviewed time-motion studies reported effort-to-pause ratios of approximately 6:1 to 13:1, effort periods of 85–290 seconds, pauses of 5–44 seconds, postmatch lactate around 10 mmol/L, and recurring fatigue reports involving forearms, fingers, wrists, and biceps brachii.
output.model_implications: Represent the profile as an intermittent grappling sport with explicit standing-entry and groundwork phases, rather than as a continuous striking or locomotor activity. [Inference] Use action labels such as stand-up/takedown attempt, guard engagement, guard pass, sweep, positional control, escape/reversal, submission attempt, and pause/reset; these are planning abstractions anchored to the reviewed scoring and time-motion categories, not a universal biomechanical taxonomy. Preserve separate intensity and pause fields because published effort-pause values vary substantially across studies and competition formats. High-confidence correction: include grip/forearm endurance and isometric handgrip fatigue as sport-relevant variables, but do not treat handgrip strength as a complete proxy for BJJ performance. High-confidence boundary: do not encode fixed percentages for time spent in any single position, universal action order, or a single metabolic-system dominance claim; evidence varies by ruleset, belt, sex, weight class, match duration, and simulated versus official competition. [Inference] Conditioning relevance may be represented as multi-component—intermittent work capacity, strength/isometric endurance, and power—while transfer from generic tests to technical success should remain an association or hypothesis, not a direct causal claim. Avoid individualized medical or training prescriptions.

output.direct_findings: [S1] In 30-m maximum-effort forward skating, the study operationalized an early acceleration phase (second stride) and a steady-state phase (sixth stride); acceleration showed greater plantar-flexor activity and hip extension, whereas steady state showed greater knee-extensor activity and hip-abduction range of motion. Higher-caliber players showed greater hip range of motion and forefoot force application in that protocol. [S1] Ice hockey game movement includes acceleration, changes of direction, sudden stopping, and crossovers, which are not well represented by restricted linear treadmill protocols. [S2] Ice hockey is characterized by forward and backward skating, speed, agility, mobility, and coordination; wearable metrics are affected by device brand/model and application, and consistent links between wearable biomechanical data and health/performance outcomes remain unclear. [S3] In eight professional games, shifts were typically 30–80 s with 2–3 min or longer recovery; the authors report frequent accelerations/decelerations, position-related differences in absolute load, and broadly similar demands after scaling by time on ice, with defensemen performing more high-threshold decelerations per minute in all periods. [S3] The study found no clear period-wide fatigue signal in its dataset, possibly because longer rest intervals occurred in the third period; this result should not be generalized to all leagues, teams, or match contexts. [S4] Across 107 studies, on-ice testing clustered around aerobic capacity, acceleration-speed, agility/change of direction, and repeated skating sprint ability; the review emphasizes context-specific protocol selection and notes that off-ice tests can have weak predictive validity for on-ice demands.
output.model_implications: Use skating as a primary movement class, with explicit forward/backward, acceleration, deceleration, stopping, crossover, and change-of-direction labels rather than treating hockey as generic linear sprinting. [High-confidence correction] Represent a skating bout as phaseable (initial acceleration versus later steady-state/glide) when the source data support stride or phase segmentation; do not infer phase from distance alone. [High-confidence correction] Preserve acceleration/deceleration event counts and rates, normalized to time on ice where possible, alongside distance and speed; absolute totals are confounded by playing time and position. [High-confidence correction] Store player position/role, sex, age/competition level, surface/protocol, sensor type, and threshold definitions as metadata because these materially limit comparability. [Inference—planning implication] Conditioning-relevance fields may include acceleration-speed, agility/change of direction, repeated-sprint ability, and aerobic capacity as assessment domains, but should not claim that any single off-ice measure transfers directly to game performance. [Boundary] Do not encode a universal shift duration, fatigue pattern, biomechanical “optimal” technique, or wearable-derived injury prediction; the evidence is protocol-, position-, population-, and device-dependent.

output.direct_findings: [S1] In 39 male players aged 14–30, overhead shots were measured from foot contact to ball release; dominant-side shots used greater anterior trunk lean and transverse shoulder rotation than non-dominant shots, while professionals showed 21% faster crosse angular velocity and higher ball speed than high-school/collegiate players. [S1] The overhead shot’s measured action cycle includes preparatory crank-back, acceleration, and follow-through; more granular descriptions divide it into approach, crank-back, stick acceleration, stick deceleration, follow-through, and recovery. [S2] Youth male overhead-shot kinematics were quantified as a distinct multi-phase movement, supporting phase-based representation but not universal values across ages, sexes, or shot types. [S3] In a comparative study of overhand, sidearm, and underhand techniques, sidearm produced significantly greater ball velocity than overhand or underhand under the study conditions; technique-specific mechanics should therefore not be collapsed into one generic shot record. [S4] In 50 Japanese national-team male players across 13 international matches, mean movement was approximately 3,800 m at 94 m/min overall; midfielders had the highest average speed and sprint distance, whereas attack and defense covered more total distance and lower-intensity acceleration/deceleration than midfielders. [S5] The literature synthesis found 120 included studies but only 14 addressing match or training demands, with substantial gaps across field, box, and sixes lacrosse; the review specifically identifies sixes as under-researched.
output.model_implications: Represent lacrosse as an intermittent, position-dependent team sport with separate locomotor and stick-skill streams; this is a high-confidence model correction supported by [S4]. Encode shooting as a phase sequence with at least approach/preparation, crank-back, acceleration, deceleration, follow-through, and recovery, while allowing missing phases for sensor-limited records; this is a high-confidence structural inference from [S1] [S2]. Keep overhand, sidearm, and underhand shots as distinct action classes rather than pooling them; this is directly supported by [S3]. Store dominant versus non-dominant side and player level as covariates for shot kinematics; this is directly supported by [S1]. Treat sprint distance, average speed, acceleration/deceleration counts, and total distance as position- and competition-format-specific rather than universal lacrosse constants; this is supported by [S4] [S5]. Conditioning relevance should remain planning inference: the observed repeated high-speed locomotion and position differences justify modeling speed, acceleration/deceleration, and intermittent-load variables, but the cited studies do not establish that any particular conditioning program improves performance. Do not generalize the male international GPS profile to women’s, youth, box, or sixes lacrosse without separate evidence; [S5] documents major evidence gaps.

output.direct_findings: [GPS/AS review] Across 51 age-grade and senior rugby-union studies, backs generally covered more total, relative, and high-speed-running distance than forwards, while forwards recorded more collisions and impacts; the most intense rolling time windows exceeded average whole-match demands. [Cunniffe et al.] In a small elite selection-game sample, players averaged 6,953 m over 83 minutes, with substantial standing/walking, jogging, cruising, striding, high-intensity running, and sprinting; the back produced more >20 km/h sprints than the forward, while the forward entered the 6–12 km/h zone more often. [Tackle biomechanics review] The tackle is a frequent in-play event, and the limited 3D literature indicates that one-on-one tackle technique can change when tackle height, leg drive, or tackle speed is modified; the review emphasizes that evidence is heterogeneous and that an optimal technique for performance or injury reduction remains unresolved. [Performance-analysis review] In professional men’s 15-a-side rugby union, isolated performance indicators are often confounded by opposition, field location, match location, and match period; collective attacking behavior has been studied, but the evidence base is less developed than simple indicator counting.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent Rugby union as an intermittent, position-dependent collision sport with separate locomotor and contact-event channels rather than as a single continuous running profile. High-confidence correction: distinguish backs and forwards for distance, high-speed running, sprint frequency, and collision/impact exposure, while retaining within-position variability. High-confidence correction: include peak/intense rolling windows as a distinct demand feature; whole-match averages should not stand in for peak phases. High-confidence correction: model action phases separately—locomotion, acceleration/deceleration, sprinting, tackle/contact, and contextual attacking/defensive phases—because the systematic reviews do not support collapsing them into one generic movement label. Inference: conditioning relevance can be represented as specificity of locomotor and contact exposure, but the cited evidence does not justify prescribing individualized loads, asserting that GPS metrics directly measure mechanical load, or claiming that a laboratory biomechanical finding transfers unchanged to live match performance. Boundary: the GPS case study is based on only two players and should calibrate action categories, not universal numeric benchmarks; rugby league, sevens, age-grade, women’s, and different competition tiers should not be silently pooled with senior men’s 15-a-side union.

output.direct_findings: [Nesbit-2005] In 84 male and 1 female amateur golfers, a full-body 3-D model showed that the golf swing is a highly coordinated, individualized motion; wrist action contributed importantly to clubhead velocity and clubface orientation, while hand trajectory and mechanical work were most closely related to skill level. [Meister-2011] In 10 professionals and 5 amateurs, downswing initiation was characterized by reversal of pelvic rotation followed by upper-torso rotation; peak X-factor preceded peak free moment, and peak free moment, X-factor, and upper-torso rotation were strongly correlated with clubhead speed in that sample. [Bourgain-2022] The literature is dominated by laboratory-based kinematic studies using heterogeneous definitions, coordinate systems, event timings, and reporting methods; the review therefore recommends methodological standardization and cautions against treating isolated kinematic variables as universal swing prescriptions. [Evans-2015] A round combines prolonged low-to-moderate activity such as walking with brief high-intensity swings; putting involves relatively little whole-body movement but sustained trunk inclination, whereas full swings involve rapid multi-segment motion. The review also notes that laboratory clubhead-speed and launch measures are indirect proxies for on-course performance. [Ehlert-2020] Across 25 intervention studies, strength-and-conditioning programs often improved clubhead speed, ball speed, and distance, with synthesized significant effects generally around 4–6.4%, but responses varied and evidence for accuracy, consistency, and direct playing outcomes was less consistent.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent Golf as a mixed-demand sport with separate movement-record classes for walking/round activity, full-swing phases, and putting/postural maintenance; do not encode it as continuous high-intensity locomotion. High-confidence correction: a full-swing record should preserve at least address, backswing, transition/initial downswing, downswing, impact, and follow-through/finish events, while allowing athlete-specific timing and kinematic variability. High-confidence correction: include pelvis-to-torso sequencing, wrist/club behavior, and ground-interaction variables as candidate observables, but do not make any single variable a universal causal rule. Inference for planning only: strength/power or mobility-related conditioning may be relevant to swing-speed and distance fields, but transfer to accuracy, injury risk, or on-course scoring must not be inferred without outcome-specific evidence. Inference for planning only: laboratory clubhead speed should be stored as a proxy/measurement context rather than equated with competitive golf performance. Boundary: evidence is concentrated in male golfers, controlled swings, and laboratory settings; avoid generalizing benchmark values across sex, age, skill level, club, or terrain without matched data.

output.direct_findings: [S1] Artistic-gymnastics biomechanics research is predominantly skill- and apparatus-specific; the review identifies take-off, flight/rotation, body configuration, apparatus interaction, and landing as important performance variables, while noting limited sport-wide generalization. [S2] The 2025 scoping review included eight landing studies and found heterogeneous protocols; landing stabilization is commonly assessed with time-to-stabilization and center-of-pressure measures, and muscle activity mainly with lower-limb surface EMG. It reports that drop height, age, training level, and task demands can affect activation patterns, but standardized strength–stability relationships were not established. [S2] Reported vertical ground-reaction-force values across gymnastics landings span approximately 7.1–15.8 body weights, varying with element height/complexity and execution; this is a literature range, not a universal per-skill constant. [S3] Gymnasts experience repeated impact landings, and loading reflects multiple interacting mechanisms, including mass distribution, segment coupling, landing technique, and regulatory constraints; the review specifically cautions that laboratory and theoretical evidence do not by themselves demonstrate field effectiveness of countermeasures. [S4] In one international-level male gymnast performing a backward somersault, the modeled landing comprised an initial phase from touchdown to peak vertical force and a terminal phase from peak force until force returned to body weight; hip, knee, and ankle flexed rapidly initially, while terminal-phase joint stiffness and measured muscle activation were several times greater than initially, with kinematic symmetry but greater kinetic and activation asymmetry. [S5] Still-rings routines are organized around swing/kip, handstand, strength/hold, swing-to-strength, and dismount elements under apparatus-specific scoring constraints; the review links rings strength/hold elements to high relative and maximal upper-extremity strength demands, while swings and dismounts involve distinct dynamic loading and timing requirements. [S6] The FIG repository is the authoritative source for the current MAG and WAG Codes of Points and therefore supports event/routine taxonomy and scoring-rule fields, not physiological or injury-risk magnitudes.
output.model_implications: Use apparatus- and action-phase labels rather than one undifferentiated gymnastics movement class: take-off/propulsion, flight/rotation, apparatus interaction or hold, and landing/stabilization. This is a high-confidence structural correction supported by [S1], [S4], and [S5]. Store landing load as a distribution/range with skill, apparatus, landing-surface, participant, and measurement-method metadata; do not encode 7.1–15.8 body weights as a universal gymnastics constant. This is a high-confidence calibration correction supported by [S2] and [S3]. Represent landing as at least touchdown-to-peak-force and post-peak recovery phases when force/EMG data are available; phase boundaries are measurement definitions, not immutable biological stages. This is a high-confidence data-model correction supported by [S4]. Preserve bilateral/asymmetry fields separately for kinematics, kinetics, and muscle activation because symmetry in one domain does not imply symmetry in another [S4]. Treat conditioning relevance—such as transfer from general strength, balance, or preconditioning exercises to skill execution—as planning inference unless a study directly tests the specific exercise, apparatus, skill, and outcome; [S2] found no established strength–activity–stabilization relationship, and [S5] is mostly element-specific. Do not infer injury prevention, performance transfer, or individualized training prescriptions from these sources alone.

output.direct_findings: [S1] The on-water evidence base comprises 27 peer-reviewed studies; reported measures cluster around time, distance, velocity, acceleration, force, power, and crew synchrony, with gate force, horizontal oar angle, and boat velocity the most frequently reported variables. [S2] Rowing performance is determined by mean shell velocity over the 2000 m race; biomechanics have been described across sculling and sweep rowing, on-water and ergometer settings, but the literature does not establish a single ideal technique or clear biomechanical predictors of 2000 m performance. [S3] In 10 collegiate male rowers tested on an ergometer at three stroke-rate bands, force-output curves and lumbopelvic kinematics changed with intensity; peak torque magnitude did not change, but its timing shifted, and anterior pelvic rotation at the catch was lower at higher rates. These observations are not sufficient to establish injury mechanisms or elite-rower generalization. [S4] Indoor-rowing lower-limb EMG work identified phase-dependent muscle activity, with vasti and soleus emphasized during the drive and tibialis anterior during recovery; this is a task-specific neuromuscular observation, not proof of conditioning transfer. [S5] USRowing defines four practical stroke parts—catch, drive, finish, and recovery—and describes a whole-body sequence in which the drive begins with leg action, followed by trunk opening and arm pull; recovery reverses the sequence toward the next catch.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent rowing as a cyclic whole-body stroke with ordered catch → drive → finish → recovery phases, rather than as an undifferentiated upper-body action. High-confidence correction: include leg-dominant early drive, sequential trunk and arm contribution, and a faster/returning recovery as phase attributes; treat exact phase percentages and joint-angle targets as configurable parameters, not universal constants. High-confidence correction: distinguish on-water shell/crew metrics (boat velocity, acceleration, oar angle, gate force, synchrony) from ergometer handle-force, seat-motion, and laboratory EMG records; do not treat them as interchangeable labels. Inference: a movement schema may include force timing, stroke rate, power, and phase coordination as calibration variables because these are repeatedly measured in the literature, but their weighting for race performance must remain sport-context and population dependent. Planning inference only: conditioning relevance can be tagged as repeated lower-limb/trunk/upper-limb coordination and force-endurance demand; the cited evidence does not justify individualized prescriptions, injury-risk predictions, or claims that ergometer findings transfer one-to-one to on-water racing.

output.direct_findings: [S1] In elite slalom, giant slalom, super-G, and downhill, performance-relevant factors include mechanical-energy conservation/dissipation, ski–snow friction, aerodynamic drag, ground-reaction force, turn radius, and ski/centre-of-mass trajectory. [S1] The review reports that technical-event performance is associated with earlier, smoother force application, suitable trajectory, and carving that reduces skidding-related frictional losses; speed-event performance is strongly affected by aerodynamic drag and low-drag posture. [S2] Alpine racing requires continuous adaptation among carving, skidding, terrain, gate setup, slope, and snow conditions; turn-cycle descriptions include weight transition, turn initiation, steering, and exit/transfer, with technique differing between slalom, giant slalom, super-G, and downhill. [S2] Peak ground-reaction forces can reach approximately five times body weight in slalom, and force magnitude/timing differs by discipline and turn phase; steering generally carries greater force than the weight-transition phase. [S3] A validated wearable differential-GNSS plus terrain/air-drag model measured external forces in World Cup giant slalom, super-G, and downhill field conditions, finding substantially different physical demands across disciplines. [S3] The study found that ski–snow friction and air drag are discipline-dependent contributors to energy dissipation and speed control, rather than interchangeable generic load variables. [S4] An interview and training-record overview of Olympic programs describes alpine racing as combining strength, strength endurance/stability, power, aerobic and anaerobic capacity, balance, coordination/motor control, and mobility, while reporting discipline-specific run durations, turn counts, and loading patterns. [S4] The overview reports approximate peak forces of 4 body weights in slalom, 3.2 in giant slalom, and 2.6 in super-G/downhill, but these are program-level summarized values and should not be treated as universal athlete thresholds.
output.model_implications: High-confidence correction: represent Skiing as discipline-specific rather than as one homogeneous movement profile; at minimum distinguish slalom, giant slalom, super-G, and downhill. High-confidence correction: encode a repeated turn cycle with weight transition/edge change, initiation, steering/loading, and exit, while allowing straight-running and jumps as separate phases, especially for speed events. High-confidence correction: include external-load channels separately for ground-reaction force, ski–snow friction, aerodynamic drag, speed, trajectory, and turn radius; do not collapse them into a single generic intensity score.
